$comment: Emission line tables for the plasma gases, and the line-selection rule for each.
SOURCE. Every line below is an observed air wavelength (nm) and relative intensity
from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database, neutral species, 380-780nm.
https://physics.nist.gov/asd
WHY THERE IS A PER-GAS `select` RULE, AND WHY THAT IS NOT A FUDGE.
ASD relative intensities are SOURCE-DEPENDENT and not radiometric. They come from
whichever reference measured that spectrum, usually an arc or a condensed discharge,
and a low-pressure glow tube populates its upper levels quite differently. Feeding
the raw table to a color integral gives neon as a muddy mauve (x=0.354 y=0.319),
because Ne's 470-540nm lines are listed at 12000-20000 against 585.2nm at 20000.
In an arc that is true. In a sign tube those levels are barely populated, which is
why neon signs are orange-red and not white.
Three candidate UNIFORM rules were tested and all three failed:
- every line as listed        -> neon mauve. Wrong.
- lowest radiating manifold   -> fixes neon, makes argon deep red. Wrong: argon's
2p->1s array is 696-853nm, where the eye scores under 0.01, so it cannot be what
sets argon's color.
- NIST Handbook persistent lines -> fits neon by coincidence, and lists NO blue
argon lines at all. Those tables are curated for detecting trace elements in an
arc, not for what a discharge looks like.
So the rule is stated per gas, with its physical justification, and each result is
checked against what that tube is documented to look like. The claim this file makes
is 'derived from cited data by a stated and reproducible method', NOT 'measured'.
A measured SPD of an actual low-pressure tube would supersede all of it.
$phosphors: THE CRT PHOSPHORS ARE A DIFFERENT KIND OF ENTRY, AND A WEAKER ONE. Read this
before trusting a number below the gases.
A gas emits LINES and this file lists them from NIST ASD, an external measured
source. A phosphor emits a BAND, and no equivalent public table of band shapes
exists — what is published for the P-numbers is the resulting CHROMATICITY
(EIA/JEDEC Publication No. 16, 'Optical Characteristics of Cathode Ray Tube
Screens', and the manufacturer data sheets behind it).
So the direction of derivation is REVERSED for these entries, and that has to
be said out loud: the gases go spectrum -> color, and the phosphors go
published color -> band. Each `bands` block below is the single energy-
Gaussian that best reproduces that phosphor's published x,y under
scripts/lib/cie.mjs. It is a BACK-SOLVED band, not a measured one.
WHICH MAKES `validate` A CONSISTENCY CHECK HERE, NOT A KNOWN-ANSWER GATE.
For neon, `validate` compares the pipeline against a color established
independently of it, and that is real evidence. For a phosphor the band was
fitted to the very coordinate it is checked against, so passing proves only
that nobody has since broken the CMF table or the integration. That is worth
having and it is not the same claim. Neon remains the pipeline's only true
known-answer gate.
WHAT IS NEVERTHELESS NON-CIRCULAR, because it was not put in by hand:
1. P1 and P39 were fitted INDEPENDENTLY, from different published
coordinates, and converged on the same band — 529nm/48nm and 529nm/52nm.
They should: P39 is P1's chemistry, Zn2SiO4:Mn with arsenic added to
lengthen the decay, not to change the color. The fit reproduced a fact
about the compounds that was never given to it.
2. P11's fitted ZnS:Ag band is reused UNCHANGED as P4's blue component and
as P7's flash layer, because all three are the same compound. P4's white
point then falls out at a residual of 0.0001. A wrong blue band would not
compose correctly into a different phosphor's white.
3. P3's fit lands at 594nm/110nm against the 'broad ~590nm band with real
green content' that src/tokens/colors.css described years earlier and in
prose. Neither number came from the other.
4. Every fitted width is physically ordinary for its compound class: the
silicates narrow (~50nm), the sulfides broad (76-130nm).
A measured SPD of a real screen would supersede all of it and should.
PERSISTENCE. `decay.to10` is the time to fall to 10% of peak emission, in
MILLISECONDS for every entry — so a microsecond-class sulfide reads 0.035 and
a long-persistence silicate reads 400. Those two live on one scale on purpose:
the four orders of magnitude between them ARE the design, and hiding them
behind per-entry units would hide the only thing distinguishing these
phosphors from each other once the color is settled.
THE PERSISTENCE CLASS IS SOLID; THE EXACT FIGURE IS NOT. That a sulfide decays
in microseconds and willemite:As in hundreds of milliseconds is the documented
reason each was fitted to the equipment it was fitted to, and nothing in this
system depends on more precision than that. The specific `to10` values are
PROVISIONAL pending a data-sheet citation per phosphor, and are marked so.

neon.label: Neon
why: REFERENCE ONLY - THIS PALETTE IS NOT GENERATED. Neon's shipped ramp predates
this script and stays hand-built, because it was solved hue-first at maximum
saturation and neither gamut strategy here reproduces it: --amber-90 is #ff6b08
with blue still at 8/255, where holding the chromaticity gives #ff6954 and
clipping gives #ff3d00. Regenerating neon would repaint the whole framework to
no one's benefit.
What neon is for is proving the pipeline. The 2p->1s array only - in a
low-pressure glow those are the lowest excited states that radiate in the
visible and are populated far more heavily than anything above them. Integrating
them gives x=0.6405 y=0.3591 against the x=0.631 y=0.369 this system derived
independently years earlier: agreement to 0.01 in xy. `validate` below turns
that into a build gate, so a change to the CIE table or the integration that
would quietly move the three real palettes fails here first, against a known
answer, instead of silently shipping.

helium.label: Helium
why: Every listed line, no cut. Helium has no low 2p->1s array to dominate the way
the heavier gases do - its visible lines all fall out of n=3 and n=4 decaying to
n=2, at comparable excitation energies, so no manifold outranks the rest and
there is nothing principled to exclude. The result is a near-white chromaticity
with a pink cast, which is what a helium tube looks like: the strong yellow at
587.6nm carries the luminance while 447.1nm and 667.8nm pull it off the
blackbody locus toward purple.

argon.label: Argon
why: Argon is the one gas here where the cut changes the answer, so it gets the
longest note.
Argon radiates most of its power in the 2p->1s array at 696-772nm, listed at
10000-25000 against 15-400 for the blue group. The CIE observer scores 750nm at
0.00012, so that array is nearly invisible however loud it is - which is exactly
why argon is DIM, and worth stating plainly: most of what argon emits is not
where the eye is.
Integrating the full table anyway lands x=0.320 y=0.147, a saturated violet-
MAGENTA, because even discounted by four orders of magnitude that array is loud
enough to drag the result red. Dropping it gives x=0.216 y=0.105 - the pale
violet-lavender an argon tube is documented to be, and what the eye reports.
The justification for dropping it is radiation trapping: the 2p->1s transitions
terminate on the 1s levels, two of which are metastable and heavily populated in
a low-pressure glow, so those photons are reabsorbed and re-emitted many times
before escaping. Optically-thin intensities like ASD's overstate what leaves the
tube. The higher transitions feeding the blue group are not trapped this way.
BE HONEST ABOUT THE STATUS OF THAT: it is a mechanism invoked to explain a
discrepancy, not one measured here. A recorded spectrum of a real low-pressure
argon tube would settle it and should replace this the day one is available.

krypton.label: Krypton
why: Every listed line, no cut, for the same reason as argon: the 758-777nm group is
loud and nearly invisible, and the observer discounts it without anyone having to
decide to. What is left is a blue-violet cluster at 427-450nm against the 557.0nm
green and the 587.1nm yellow, which integrates close to white with a violet cast.
NOTE: 587.09nm at 3000 is the strongest VISIBLE krypton line, not 557.03 at 2000.

p1.label: P1
why: Zn2SiO4:Mn — willemite, the oldest CRT phosphor and the one the early
oscilloscopes and radar indicators were built around. A silicate host, so a
narrow band: 48nm against the sulfides' 76-130nm.
Fitted independently of P39 and landed on the same band, which is the check
that matters here — see note 1 in $phosphors.

p3.label: P3
why: REFERENCE ONLY - THIS PALETTE IS NOT GENERATED, on exactly the same footing
as neon and for the same reason. P3's ramp is the one the source design
system was drawn against; regenerating it would repaint every amber screen
in the framework to settle a question that is already settled.
What it IS here for is --gas-scatter. That token has been carrying neon's
1.00 as an admitted placeholder since the gas pass, because a band has
nothing for a line integral to run over. It does now, and the number is
derived rather than borrowed.
The fit landing at 594nm/110nm against the 'broad ~590nm band with real
green content' that colors.css has described in prose since long before
this file existed is note 3 in $phosphors.

p4.label: P4
why: The television phosphor, and the reason monochrome sets looked white rather
than any one color: a BLEND of ZnS:Ag blue and (Zn,Cd)S:Ag yellow, mixed to
sit near the white point. Two bands, one screen, one decay — which is what
separates it from P7 and is worth being precise about, because 'two
emitters' describes both and means something different in each.
P4 is two powders MIXED, emitting together, and the eye integrates them into
white. P7 is two powders LAYERED, emitting in sequence, and the eye sees the
color change with time. A blend has one color; a cascade has two.
The blue component is P11's fitted band, reused unchanged because it is the
same compound. Only the yellow band and the mix ratio were fitted, and the
white point then falls out at a residual of 0.0001 — note 2 in $phosphors.
Later tubes replaced the cadmium sulfide with ZnS:Cu,Al on health grounds,
which moves the yellow band slightly. This entry is the original.

p7.label: P7
p7.appearance: blue flash over a yellow-green afterglow
why: THE RADAR PHOSPHOR, and the only entry in this file whose color is not one
color. Two coatings, not a mixture:
ZnS:Ag        the FLASH. A blue layer facing the beam, decaying in tens of
microseconds. This is what the beam writes.
(Zn,Cd)S:Cu   the AFTERGLOW. A yellow-green layer behind it, decaying over
hundreds of milliseconds with a visible tail running to
seconds. This is what the screen holds.
`cascade: true` records the mechanism, and it is the reason the two are not
independently driven: the beam excites the blue layer, and the BLUE LAYER'S
OWN PHOTONS pump the yellow-green one behind it. The afterglow is downstream
of the flash, so it can never appear without it and always outlives it.
WHY THIS WAS WORTH BUILDING. A radar PPI sweeps once every few seconds. A
single-layer phosphor either decays before the sweep comes round — leaving
nothing to look at — or persists so long the display smears into an unusable
blur. P7 does both jobs with two materials: a sharp bright blue mark at the
instant of the sweep, and a slowly-fading yellow-green trail behind it that
is still legible when the beam returns. The operator reads position from the
flash and history from the glow, in one glance.
WHAT IT MEANS FOR THIS SYSTEM. `bands` is the flash and drives the --emit-*
ramp, because the flash is what a beam WRITES and therefore what text is.
`afterglow.bands` drives --gas-* and the ghost hue, because the glow is what
the screen HOLDS. That split is not an interpretation of the hardware, it is
the hardware, and it inverts the rule at the top of src/tokens/effects.css
that the halo tracks the emitter — which is true of every other entry here
and false of this one by construction.
It also predicts the look correctly, which is the part worth checking. On a
real P7 tube static text is rewritten sixty times a second, so it is
CONTINUOUSLY flashed blue and CONTINUOUSLY pumping the layer beneath: static
text reads as blue-white ink inside a yellow-green halo. Text that stops
being rewritten loses the blue on the very next frame and leaves the
yellow-green behind for seconds. Both fall straight out of the ink/halo
split above without anything being special-cased.

p11.label: P11
why: ZnS:Ag. A photographic-recording phosphor: blue is where film emulsion is
most sensitive, so P11 was fitted to tubes whose screens were meant to be
photographed rather than watched.
Watched, it is the worst screen in this file, and for a reason the system
should render rather than hide. It decays in tens of microseconds — three
orders below a refresh interval — so the screen is genuinely dark between
frames and the flicker is at maximum. Short persistence and heavy flicker
are the same fact; see the modulation-depth note in scripts/derive-gas.mjs.
Its fitted band is the ZnS:Ag reference for this file, reused unchanged in
P4 and in P7's flash layer.

p31.label: P31
why: ZnS:Cu — the green everybody actually pictures when they picture a terminal
or a laboratory oscilloscope. The highest luminous efficiency of any
phosphor here, sitting near the peak of the photopic curve, which is why it
displaced the willemites for anything meant to be looked at directly.
A sulfide, so a broad band (78nm) against P1's silicate 48nm, and that width
is what pulls it off the spectral locus to a green a screen can actually be
rather than a laser line.

p39.label: P39
why: Zn2SiO4:Mn,As — P1's willemite with arsenic added. The arsenic lengthens the
decay by orders of magnitude and leaves the color where it was, which is
why this entry and P1 fit to the same band from different published
coordinates (note 1 in $phosphors).
Fitted to slow-refresh terminals and radar indicators for one reason: at a
decay of hundreds of milliseconds the screen is still near full brightness
when the next refresh arrives, so there is no flicker to see at any refresh
rate. It buys that with smear — anything that moves drags a tail. That trade
is the whole character of the phosphor and both halves come off one number.
`model: becquerel` marks the decay as a power law, I = I0/(1+t/t0)^n, rather
than an exponential. Long-persistence phosphors have a fast knee and a very
long tail, which no single cubic-bezier can express — the reason the CSS
emits a sampled linear() easing instead.
